title: Authentication
subtitle: Watch a user prove who they are with a password, a session or token, an OAuth login, and a second factor.
learn: Why passwords are stored as slow salted hashes, never as text or fast hashes
How server-side sessions and signed JWTs differ, and what each costs you
The OAuth 2.0 / OIDC authorization-code login flow, hop by hop
How MFA adds a second factor and why phishing-resistant factors matter
How short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens limit the damage of theft

steps.title: Who is this, really?
steps.body: HTTP is stateless: every request arrives with no memory of the last one. So how does the server know the person clicking Pay is the same person who logged in a minute ago, and that they are who they claim to be at all? Authentication answers 'who are you?'. This lesson follows one login from the first password to the tokens that keep you logged in.
steps.idea: Authentication proves identity once, then hands the client something cheaper to present on every later request.
steps.caption: A browser, an app, and no proof of identity yet.

steps.title: Check the password without keeping it
steps.body: The browser sends the password over TLS. The app looks up the user's row, then hashes the submitted password with that user's random salt and compares it to the stored hash. The hash must be deliberately slow and memory-hungry, such as Argon2id, bcrypt or scrypt, tuned to roughly 100 ms per attempt. A fast hash like plain SHA-256 lets an attacker test billions of guesses per second.
steps.idea: Store a per-user salted, slow hash; the server never needs the password again after checking it.
steps.caption: App fetches the stored salt+hash and compares.

steps.title: Option A: a server-side session
steps.body: The password matched, so the app creates a random 128-bit session ID, saves it in a session store such as Redis along with the user ID, and sends it back in a cookie marked HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite. On every later request the browser sends the cookie and the app does one store lookup. Logging out or banning someone is simply deleting the record.
steps.idea: A session is an opaque ID pointing at server state, so revocation is instant but every request costs a lookup.
steps.caption: Session ID stored server-side, cookie sent to the browser.

steps.title: Option B: a signed JWT
steps.body: Instead of storing state, the app can issue a JSON Web Token: claims such as user ID and expiry, signed with a key. Any service holding the matching key can verify it with no database call, which suits many microservices. The price is that the token is valid until it expires. You cannot easily revoke one early, so access tokens are kept short, around 15 minutes.
steps.idea: JWTs trade revocability for stateless verification; keep them short-lived because you cannot take them back.
steps.caption: Signed token verified locally, no store lookup.

steps.title: Log in with someone else's identity
steps.body: With 'Sign in with Google', your app never sees the password. The browser is redirected to the identity provider (IdP), the user logs in there, and the IdP redirects back with a short-lived one-time authorization code. Your server swaps that code, plus its client secret and a PKCE verifier, for an ID token (OIDC, who the user is) and an access token. The code, not the tokens, travels through the browser.
steps.idea: OAuth/OIDC delegates the password to a specialist; your app only exchanges a one-time code for tokens over a back channel.
steps.caption: Redirect out, code back, tokens via the back channel.

steps.title: Add a second factor
steps.body: A password alone can be phished, guessed or reused from another breach. MFA requires something else: a one-time code from an authenticator app, a push approval, or a passkey (WebAuthn) bound to a hardware key or device. Passkeys sign a challenge tied to the real website's domain, so a fake lookalike site cannot trick the user into handing over a usable code. SMS codes are better than nothing but can be SIM-swapped.
steps.idea: Require a second, independent factor, and prefer phishing-resistant ones like passkeys over typed codes.
steps.caption: Login pauses until the second factor checks out.

steps.title: Stay logged in without long-lived access
steps.body: A 15-minute access token would log users out constantly, so the login also returns a refresh token that lasts days or weeks. When the access token expires, the client sends the refresh token to get a new pair. Good practice is rotation: each refresh token works once, and if an old one is replayed the server revokes the whole chain. The refresh token lives in a server-checked store, so it can be revoked.
steps.idea: Short access tokens limit exposure; a revocable, rotating refresh token provides the long session.
steps.caption: Expired access token swapped for a fresh pair.

steps.title: The user table leaks
steps.body: Suppose an attacker dumps the whole user database. With slow salted hashes, each password must be guessed one at a time: at 100 ms per try, that is only 10 guesses per second per CPU core, and salts stop one guess from checking every user at once. Strong passwords survive; weak ones fall. Plain-text or unsalted MD5 would have exposed everyone immediately, and reused passwords would be tried on other sites.
steps.idea: Assume the database will leak one day; slow salted hashes plus MFA turn a breach into a slow, partial problem.
steps.caption: Stolen hashes are expensive to crack.

steps.title: The whole login
steps.body: Check the password against a slow salted hash, or delegate to an IdP with the OAuth/OIDC code flow. Add MFA, ideally a passkey. Then issue either a server-side session cookie or a short-lived signed token with a rotating refresh token. Sessions favor easy revocation, JWTs favor stateless verification, and many real systems combine both. What a logged-in user is allowed to do is authorization, a separate lesson.
steps.idea: Prove identity once with strong factors, then carry it in something short-lived and revocable.
steps.caption: Password or IdP, second factor, then tokens.

quiz.q: Why is bcrypt or Argon2id a better password hash than SHA-256?
options: It produces a shorter output that is cheaper to store
It is reversible, so support staff can recover forgotten passwords
It is deliberately slow and tunable, so brute-forcing a leaked table is expensive
It removes the need for a salt
quiz.why: Password hashes are meant to be slow and memory-hard so attackers cannot test billions of guesses per second. They are not reversible, and salts are still used (usually built in).

quiz.q: A user reports their laptop was stolen and you must log them out everywhere right now. Which design makes that easiest?
options: Server-side sessions: delete the user's session records
Self-contained JWTs valid for 24 hours with no server state
quiz.why: Sessions live on the server, so deleting them ends access immediately. A stateless JWT stays valid until it expires unless you add a denylist, which brings back server state.

quiz.q: In the OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow, why does the browser carry only a one-time code instead of the access token?
options: Codes are larger and carry more claims
The token is exchanged server-to-server with the client secret or PKCE verifier, so a code intercepted in the browser is useless alone
Browsers cannot store tokens at all
It lets the IdP skip authenticating the user
quiz.why: The code is short-lived and single-use, and redeeming it requires proof only your server (or the original client via PKCE) has, so the tokens never pass through the URL.

quiz.q: An attacker runs a fake login page that relays whatever the user types, including a 6-digit authenticator code, to the real site in real time. Which second factor best defeats this?
quiz.why: Passkeys sign a challenge bound to the genuine site's domain, so a lookalike domain gets nothing usable. Typed codes can be relayed by the phishing page.

cheatsheet.def: Random per-user value mixed into the password before hashing, so identical passwords hash differently and precomputed tables fail.
Slow, tunable password hashes. Aim for roughly 100 ms per hash on your hardware; raise the cost as hardware improves.
Random opaque ID pointing at server-side state. Set HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite. Instantly revocable, costs a lookup per request.
Signed token holding claims and an expiry. Verified without a lookup, but valid until it expires. Keep access tokens ~5-15 minutes.
OAuth 2.0 delegates access to resources; OpenID Connect adds an ID token on top that says who the user is. Use the code flow with PKCE.
Each refresh token is single-use and replaced on refresh; replaying an old one signals theft and revokes the chain.
A second independent factor. Passkeys (WebAuthn) are phishing-resistant because they are bound to the site's domain.
Authentication: who are you. Authorization: what may you do. Do the first, then the second, as separate checks.
